title: Country from Coordinates Finder
description: Get the country containing a bare coordinate pair with the Country from Coordinates Finder — boundary data, honest about water and borders. Free.
summary_sentence: For example, 40.7580, −73.9855 answers 'United States' from boundary data alone — while a point a mile offshore answers with the honest emptiness of open water.
quick_answer: The Country from Coordinates Finder gives a quick, unambiguous answer for a bare coordinate pair: the country containing the point, taken from OpenStreetMap's address record. Paste the pair and read the country — including an honest open-water result for ocean points instead of a borrowed nearest nation.
steps_intro: Two numbers in, one country out — with the edges handled honestly:

body.t: A coordinates file claiming a country column gets verified point by point — the
adds the full record around each verdict.
Which country was this GPS cluster in? The pair answers before the album gets captioned wrong.
Near frontiers, the point's country can differ from the trip's headline country — worth knowing before roaming charges explain it.
Click Lesotho inside South Africa, or Baarle's patchwork, and watch 'country' stop being a colouring-book word.
Mid-ocean points return no country — labelled as open water rather than assigned to the nearest coast. A finder willing to say 'none' is one whose 'United States' you can trust.
Where borders are contested, the record follows OpenStreetMap's documented position. The answer is the map data's, offered as such — the disputes belong to diplomacy, and the page's FAQs say so.

faq: What about points at sea?
Open-ocean points return an honest empty result ('open water' style), not the nearest country. Near coasts, the record follows the boundary data's shoreline treatment.
Are disputed borders handled?
They are reported as the dataset holds them — OpenStreetMap documents its approach to disputed boundaries, and this finder reflects that record rather than adjudicating.
Which datum do these coordinate tools use?
WGS84 pairs, as GPS and web maps produce them.
Do more decimal places always mean better accuracy?
The country verdict is stable across decimals except within metres of a border, where the point's own accuracy becomes the story.
Can I copy the result into GIS software?
The country name is an attribute — copy it beside the coordinates in your dataset; the pair itself is already GIS-ready.
Territorial waters?
Boundary datasets centre on land. A point just offshore can read no-country while lying in territorial waters — the dataset's scope, stated rather than hidden.
Embassies and military bases?
Soil follows the host country in boundary data; legal status is a longer story that no finder settles.
Antarctica?
No sovereign country — the treaty continent returns the honest absence.
Two answers from two apps?
Different boundary vintages or dispute positions. Note both sources; for anything official, governments outrank apps.
City and region too?
The Coordinates Lookup Tool returns the full stack; this page is the country slice, kept deliberately single-purpose.
Island nations?
Archipelagos resolve island by island from their boundaries — a point between islands at sea can honestly return none.
